job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Wei Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a bench in Porto most days, testing circuit boards for electric car chargers. I plug them in, run them through heat and load, and write up what failed. My boss Inês gives me the boards and Rui, the technician next to me, shows me the tricks the textbook didn't. I finished electrical engineering last summer with a plain pass and no internship, so this job is my whole experience. After work I go home to the flat I share with my cousin Tiago, and we cook badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, I've got work and the bench isn't going anywhere. At work Rui and I would joke that the hype crowd owes us lunch. Online I'd say it's a reminder that tech companies sell stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it wouldn't change much for me. I test charger boards for electric cars, and AI only helps with the write-up, so a quiet year would suit me fine. My real stress is my 450 euro share of the rent and a loan I'm still working out how to repay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep testing, and keep asking Inês for harder boards. I'd go on using the chatbot for datasheet questions, like I do now, and put 150 euros a month into savings. I'd also finally sign up for the evening course in power electronics I've been eyeing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly. A bit bored by the whole debate, but calm about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the loan. How worried are you about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very. It's around 14,000 euros and I pay 180 a month, and my dad says that's a loan you can live with. What worries me more is the rent, because Tiago and I share a two-bedroom flat and the landlord already hinted at 10 percent more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm okay. He drives a bus and has been in the union thirty years, so he'd ask whether my firm has a works council. I'd say yes, but only five people sit on it. He'd be glad, because he worries firms treat graduates as disposable.

Online I'd say tech companies sell **stories**.

My real stress is a **450 euro** rent share and a loan I'm still working out.

Put **150 euros** a month into savings.
Start the evening course in power electronics.
feel: Calm but a bit bored by the debate, with **rent** nagging in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say employers should share the gains. If software does the writing and checking, a shorter working week is the obvious thing to ask for. At work I'd say let's use it on reports and keep people on the bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My test reports and data checks would go to software first, and that's maybe a third of my week. The bench part stays human for a long while because someone has to plug the boards in. I think Inês would hire one fewer junior next year, and I'd hope to be the one she keeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly instead of just now and then. I'd ask Inês to let me build a script that writes the test reports, so I'm the person who owns it. I'd push the works council to ask about training, and put 200 euros a month away. I'd take the power electronics course too, because nobody can plug a board in from the cloud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but curious. It's a bit like when the factory got its first test robot and everyone argued, and then the job turned out to be fixing the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd own the test reports. Why would the firm let you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it saves Inês two hours a day and she hates paperwork. If I show it works, she'll protect me, at least until the next change comes along. It isn't a guarantee, but it's better than hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about being the person who automates it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm automating away my next colleague. I'd be happy to automate my own reports, but I'd feel awful if that meant the firm never hires the next graduate. I'd bring it up with the works council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a joke and it should be a political emergency. I'd say it online and at my dad's union meeting. At work I'd just say we should keep the humans on the bench for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. By 2028 the writing, checking and design are done by AI, and I'm a plain-pass graduate with a few months of experience. The bench work lasts until about 2031, and then I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save 350 euros a month, keep my room in the flat, and learn to maintain the test machines, since hands-on lasts longer. I'd ask my dad to put me in touch with the transport union, because they've dealt with automation before. If I'm let go, I'd go home to Gaia, where my parents have a spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan but not much trust in it. My stomach would do the thing it did before my final exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the plan, in one sentence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get good at the one part of the job that robots reach last: setting up and fixing real equipment, in person. Then, if work dries up, there's a spare room at my parents' and a union that might still negotiate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tiago say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tiago works in a warehouse, so he'd laugh and say he has until 2031. But he'd also be the first to lose his share of the rent if I moved back home, so we'd have to talk about the lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a window. I'd say let's use it to get a training deal and a shorter week into the firm's contract. At work I'd keep helping Rui and keep my opinions short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly hopeful. By 2031 I'd be 27, and with the power electronics course and some years on the bench I'd be useful. The reports will go to AI, but someone needs to understand what the boards do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the evening course, sit the licence exam that covers site work, and use AI for everything except the part where I touch a board. I'd save 250 euros a month and maybe look at a bigger firm that has a graduate path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. Like waiting for test results that are probably fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd be panicking and hoarding. With five years I'd be investing in skills instead of hoarding money, because I can afford to be wrong. Two years doesn't let you be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That unions should push for retraining funds now, while they still have bargaining power. He'd agree, then tell me about when the bus company brought in ticket machines and everyone thought drivers would vanish. They didn't, they just got fewer, and the ones who stayed learned the new thing.

At work I'd keep helping Rui and keep my opinions short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty, honestly. I'd say it's a good moment to rebuild how we train people, with proper apprenticeships and public support. At work I'd say let's plan, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, even better off. By 2036 I'd be 32, a senior test engineer or maybe running a small lab, and machines would do the dull parts. The only thing I'd watch is whether young graduates still get a first job at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, take the power electronics course, and do a master's part time. I'd save 200 euros a month toward a deposit on a small flat. I'd keep using AI for reports, since by then everyone will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A little excited about what lab work could become.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people would stop paying attention. For ten years everyone says it's coming, and then it comes and the firms act surprised. I'd want the union to keep reminding them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the bench look like in 2036, in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quieter, cleaner, and with fewer people on it. The boards would be tested by machines I set up, and my job would be telling the machines what good looks like, as long as there's still a first rung for the next kid. I like that picture.

At work I'd say plan, not panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years is too short to learn anything new properly. I'd be 24 with a plain degree and a few months on a bench. What would help is a union deal on retraining and a government that says out loud what it will do for people who lose work, before it happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say technology isn't the enemy, bosses who treat it as a way to cut people are. My dad drives a bus and has been in the union thirty years, and he taught me to ask who gains. If the answer is only the owners, then we have a problem.

headlineQuote: Technology isn't the enemy, bosses who treat it as a way to cut people are.
portrait: **Wei**, 22, tests charger boards in Porto, shares a flat with his cousin Tiago and carries a modest **student loan**.
Progressive and raised by a union-member bus driver, he asks **who gains** from every change and trusts collective deals.
He uses chatbots now and then for datasheets and is willing to learn more once a tool is **proven**.
His mood moves from uneasy to anxious in the two-year world, then settles to calm when he has ten years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, with a plain degree and only a few months on the bench.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** on retraining and a public plan for people who lose work.
Firms that keep hiring a **first rung** of graduates.
